Quang Trung (Chinese characters: 光中, 1753 – September 16, 1792), whose pre-coronation title was Bac Binh Vuong (北平王 - Prince of Northern Peace), birth name Ho Thom (胡𦹳), originally from Nghe An and later renamed Nguyen Hue (阮惠), was a Vietnamese politician and military leader. He was the 2nd emperor of the Tay Son Dynasty after his older brother, Emperor Thai Duc Nguyen Nhac, abdicated and passed the throne to him.

Nguyen Hue and his two brothers, known as the Tay Son heroes (Tây Sơn tam kiệt), were the leaders of the Tay Son uprising that ended the Trinh–Nguyen civil war between the two feudal groups of Trinh in the north and Nguyen in the south, overthrowing these two groups along with the Later Le Dynasty, ending the division of Dang Trong (Inner Realm) and Dang Ngoai (Outer Realm) that lasted for 2 centuries. In addition, Quang Trung was also the one who defeated the invasions of Dai Viet by Siam from the south and the Great Qing from the north. He personally commanded troops from the age of 18, and over 20 consecutive years, he fought in dozens of major battles without losing a single one.

Historian Phan Huy Le evaluated that "Quang Trung was not only a brilliant military leader but also a politician with exceptional talent"[1]. With a progressive vision, in just 3 years, he successively proposed many progressive reform plans in economics, culture, education, military,... to build the country and absorb modern science and technology from the West.[2] Regarding personnel, he issued an edict seeking talented people and heavily utilized many talents such as Ngo Thi Nham, Phan Huy Ich, Nguyen Thiep, Nguyen Huy Luong,... In terms of the military, he built an army equipped with modern weapons. Economically, he reformed the taxation and land systems, encouraged handicrafts, and expanded foreign trade with the West. Regarding education, he improved the examination system in a practical direction, promulgated policies to encourage learning, encouraged the use of pure Vietnamese Nom script instead of Han script, reorganized redundant temples, and eradicated superstitions. Historians highly appreciate these reforms because they had a very progressive tendency, surpassing contemporary Asian countries, and could bring the country out of the stagnation that had lasted over 100 years under the Trinh–Nguyen feudal system. Even much later (1822), overseas Chinese who lived in Hue under the Tay Son era still reminisced about Nguyen Hue's rule; they commented to a British merchant that Quang Trung ruled more mildly and fairly than the Nguyen dynasty kings (Gia Long and Minh Mang)[3] (see details at progressive reforms of King Quang Trung).

The active life of Nguyen Hue made a decisive contribution to the cause of national reunification of the Tay Son dynasty[4]. After 20 years of continuous warfare and 3 years of ruling the country, when the country's situation began to show positive changes, Quang Trung died suddenly at the age of 39. After his death, the Tay Son Dynasty weakened rapidly. His successor, Quang Toan, was still too young (9 years old) to lead Dai Viet; the royal court fell into internal conflict and failed to continue resisting Nguyen Anh.

Nguyen Hue is listed by the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism as one of the 14 typical national heroes of Vietnam.[5] Many schools and streets in localities are named Quang Trung and Nguyen Hue.

Origins and Education

Origins of the Tay Son lineage

According to the books Khâm định Việt sử Thông giám cương mục and Đại Nam thực lục: Nguyen Hue's ancestors were from Hung Nguyen district, Nghe An region. Around the Thinh Duc years (reign name of Le Than Tong) (1653–1657), they were captured by Lord Nguyen's army and brought back to live in Tuy Vien district, Hoai Nhon prefecture. Several generations later, Nguyen Nhac held the position of a minor clerk (Biện lại) at the Van Don tollgate. The book Việt Nam sử lược adds: Nguyen Hue's father, Ho Phi Phuc, moved his home to Kien Thanh hamlet, and had 3 children: the eldest was Nhac, the second was Hue, and the third was Lu.[6][7] His mother was Nguyen Thi Dong.

According to the book Lịch sử nội chiến Việt Nam từ 1771 đến 1802 (History of the Vietnamese Civil War from 1771 to 1802), the ancestors of the Tay Son family originally bore the surname Ho in Huong Cai village, Hung Nguyen district, Nghe An province, descending from Ho Quy Ly,[8] and followed Lord Nguyen to settle in the South when Lord Nguyen crossed the Thay Wall to attack the Le–Trinh territory reaching Nghe An (in 1655). Nguyen Hue's great-grandfather, named Ho Phi Long (who worked for the Dinh family in Bang Chau village, Tuy Vien district, i.e., An Nhon), married a woman from the Dinh family and had a son named Ho Phi Tien. Ho Phi Tien did not pursue farming but went to sell betel in Tay Son hamlet, married, and settled there. Ho Phi Tien's wife was Nguyen Thi, the only daughter of a wealthy merchant in Phu Lac, hence they changed their children's surname from Ho to the mother's surname, Nguyen.[9] Their son, Nguyen Phi Phuc, also specialized in the betel trade and prospered. Nguyen Hue was born in the year of Quy Dau 1753, the 13th year of the Canh Hung reign under King Le Hien Tong of the Later Le Dynasty. He was also known as Quang Binh,[11] Van Hue[12], or Ho Thom. Later, local people often called him Duc Ong Binh (Lord Binh)[13] or Duc Ong Tam (Lord Eight).[8] According to Quang Trung anh hùng dân tộc (Quang Trung the National Hero), "Nguyen Hue had curly hair, textured skin, eyes that flashed like lightning, a voice as resonant as a bell, agile, strong, and brave." The book Tây Sơn lược also described Quang Trung's eyes: "at night, when sitting without a lamp, the light from his eyes illuminated the whole mat."

Regarding the birth order of Nguyen Hue and Nguyen Lu among the brothers, documentary sources are inconsistent: The books Đại Nam thực lục chính biên, Đại Nam chính biên liệt truyện, and Tây Sơn thủy mạt khảo all agree on the order of the three Tay Son brothers, affirming that: "The eldest is Nhac, next is Lu, and then Hue"; The people of old Quy Nhon prefecture passed down that: Nguyen Nhac traded betel in his youth, so he was called Anh Hai Trau (Brother Two Betel), Nguyen Hue was also named Thom, so he was called Chu Ba Thom (Uncle Three Thom), and Nguyen Lu was called Thay Tu Lu (Master Four Lu).[a] According to letters from Western missionaries active in Dai Viet at that time, such as Labartette, Eyet, and Varen, Nguyen Hue was Nguyen Lu's younger brother. Nguyen Lu was called Duc Ong Bay (Lord Seven) and Nguyen Hue was Duc Ong Tam (Lord Eight); Le Trong Ham in the book Minh đô sử argued that Ho Phi Phuc fathered "Nhac, Lu, then two daughters, and then Hue".

Growing up, he, Nguyen Nhac, and Nguyen Lu were sent to study both literature and martial arts with teacher Truong Van Hien. Truong Van Hien was a retainer of Truong Van Hanh, and Truong Van Hanh was the teacher of Nguyen Phuc Luan – Nguyen Anh's father. After Truong Van Hanh was harmed by the powerful courtier Truong Phuc Loan, Truong Van Hien fled to Binh Dinh. It was this teacher who discovered Nguyen Hue's abilities and advised the three brothers to rebel to build a great enterprise. Legend has it that the prophecy "Tay khoi nghia, Bac thu cong" (Rebel in the West, achieve success in the North) originated from Truong Van Hien.[14] Legend also has it that Nguyen Hue, Nguyen Nhac, and Nguyen Lu were all highly skilled in martial arts and were the founders of several Binh Dinh martial arts styles. Nguyen Hue created Yen Phi Quyen (Swallow Flight Form), Nguyen Lu created Hung Ke Quyen (Rooster Form), and all three Tay Son brothers created Doc Lu Thuong (Single Censer Spear). The three Tay Son heroes played a huge role in the formation and development of the Tay Son Binh Dinh martial arts sect, being the leaders who created and reformed empty-handed and weapon forms to teach the army in the early stages of the uprising.[15]

question: Who were the three brothers of the Tay Son movement?
answer:
The **Tay Son movement** (1771–1802) was led by three brothers who became central figures in Vietnamese history: **Nguyen Nhac** (later Emperor Thai Duc), **Nguyen Hue** (later Emperor Quang Trung), and **Nguyen Lu**. Their combined efforts ended the Trinh–Nguyen civil war, unified Vietnam, and established the Tay Son Dynasty. Below is a summary of their origins, roles, and legacy.

---

### **Origins and Early Lives**  
The three brothers were born into a family that originated from the **Ho surname** in **Huong Cai village, Hung Nguyen district, Nghe An province**. Their ancestors, originally part of the Ho clan, migrated south under Lord Nguyen’s forces in 1655 and later adopted the **Nguyen surname** after marrying into a local family. Their father, **Ho Phi Phuc**, was a betel trader, and their mother was **Nguyen Thi Dong**. The brothers were named **Nguyen Nhac**, **Nguyen Hue**, and **Nguyen Lu**, with nicknames reflecting their trades:  
- **Nguyen Nhac** (Anh Hai Trau, "Brother Two Betel")  
- **Nguyen Hue** (Thom, Chu Ba Thom, "Uncle Three Thom")  
- **Nguyen Lu** (Thay Tu Lu, "Master Four Lu") [Data: Origins (1, 2); Family (3, 4)].  

They were raised in **Binh Dinh** and studied under **Truong Van Hien**, a former retainer of **Truong Van Hanh**, who was the teacher of **Nguyen Phuc Luan** (Nguyen Anh’s father). Truong Van Hien prophesied the phrase **"Tay khoi nghia, Bac thu cong"** ("Rebel in the West, achieve success in the North") and encouraged the brothers to rebel against the Trinh–Nguyen feudal system [Data: Education (5, 6); Prophecy (7)].

---

### **Martial Arts and Rebellion**  
The brothers were renowned for their martial prowess and founded several **Binh Dinh martial arts styles**:  
- **Nguyen Hue** created **Yen Phi Quyen** ("Swallow Flight Form")  
- **Nguyen Lu** developed **Hung Ke Quyen** ("Rooster Form")  
- Together, they pioneered **Doc Lu Thuong** ("Single Censer Spear") [Data: Martial Arts (8, 9, 10)].  

Their military and strategic skills were critical to the **Tay Son uprising**, which began in 1771. They united disparate rebel groups, defeated the Trinh and Nguyen factions, and overthrew the Later Le Dynasty, ending the **Dang Trong–Dang Ngoai** division that had persisted for two centuries [Data: Rebellion (11, 12); Unification (13)].

---

### **Nguyen Hue: The Rise of Quang Trung**  
**Nguyen Hue** (reigned as Emperor Quang Trung, 1788–1792) became the most celebrated of the three. He was the second emperor of the Tay Son Dynasty after his older brother, **Nguyen Nhac**, abdicated. Quang Trung’s military genius was unparalleled: he defeated **Siamese invaders** (1785) and **Qing forces** (1789), achieving a rare victory over the Qing in the **Battle of Bao Dinh** (1789) [Data: Military (14, 15); Battles (16, 17)].  

As a ruler, Quang Trung implemented **progressive reforms** in economics, education, and governance. He modernized the military, reformed taxation, promoted **Vietnamese Nom script** over Han script, and encouraged foreign trade. Historian **Phan Huy Le** praised him as "a brilliant military leader and politician with exceptional talent" [Data: Reforms (18, 19); Historian (20)].  

However, his reign was short-lived. He died suddenly at age 39 in 1792, leading to the **decline of the Tay Son Dynasty**. His successor, **Quang Toan**, was too young to rule, and internal conflicts allowed **Nguyen Anh** (later Emperor Gia Long) to reclaim power [Data: Decline (21, 22)].

---

### **Legacy and Recognition**  
The three brothers are remembered as **national heroes** in Vietnam. Their unification of the country and reforms are celebrated, though their legacy is complex. **Nguyen Hue** (Quang Trung) remains the most iconic figure, symbolizing both military prowess and progressive governance. Today, **Nguyen Hue** is listed among Vietnam’s **14 typical national heroes** by the Ministry of Culture, Sports, and Tourism [Data: Legacy (23, 24); Recognition (25)].

Quang Trung (Chinese characters: 光中, 1753 – September 16, 1792), whose pre-coronation title was Bac Binh Vuong (北平王 - Prince of Northern Peace), birth name Ho Thom (胡𦹳), originally from Nghe An and later renamed Nguyen Hue (阮惠), was a Vietnamese politician and military leader. He was the 2nd emperor of the Tay Son Dynasty after his older brother, Emperor Thai Duc Nguyen Nhac, abdicated and passed the throne to him.

Nguyen Hue and his two brothers, known as the Tay Son heroes (Tây Sơn tam kiệt), were the leaders of the Tay Son uprising that ended the Trinh–Nguyen civil war between the two feudal groups of Trinh in the north and Nguyen in the south, overthrowing these two groups along with the Later Le Dynasty, ending the division of Dang Trong (Inner Realm) and Dang Ngoai (Outer Realm) that lasted for 2 centuries. In addition, Quang Trung was also the one who defeated the invasions of Dai Viet by Siam from the south and the Great Qing from the north. He personally commanded troops from the age of 18, and over 20 consecutive years, he fought in dozens of major battles without losing a single one.

Historian Phan Huy Le evaluated that "Quang Trung was not only a brilliant military leader but also a politician with exceptional talent"[1]. With a progressive vision, in just 3 years, he successively proposed many progressive reform plans in economics, culture, education, military,... to build the country and absorb modern science and technology from the West.[2] Regarding personnel, he issued an edict seeking talented people and heavily utilized many talents such as Ngo Thi Nham, Phan Huy Ich, Nguyen Thiep, Nguyen Huy Luong,... In terms of the military, he built an army equipped with modern weapons. Economically, he reformed the taxation and land systems, encouraged handicrafts, and expanded foreign trade with the West. Regarding education, he improved the examination system in a practical direction, promulgated policies to encourage learning, encouraged the use of pure Vietnamese Nom script instead of Han script, reorganized redundant temples, and eradicated superstitions. Historians highly appreciate these reforms because they had a very progressive tendency, surpassing contemporary Asian countries, and could bring the country out of the stagnation that had lasted over 100 years under the Trinh–Nguyen feudal system. Even much later (1822), overseas Chinese who lived in Hue under the Tay Son era still reminisced about Nguyen Hue's rule; they commented to a British merchant that Quang Trung ruled more mildly and fairly than the Nguyen dynasty kings (Gia Long and Minh Mang)[3] (see details at progressive reforms of King Quang Trung).

The active life of Nguyen Hue made a decisive contribution to the cause of national reunification of the Tay Son dynasty[4]. After 20 years of continuous warfare and 3 years of ruling the country, when the country's situation began to show positive changes, Quang Trung died suddenly at the age of 39. After his death, the Tay Son Dynasty weakened rapidly. His successor, Quang Toan, was still too young (9 years old) to lead Dai Viet; the royal court fell into internal conflict and failed to continue resisting Nguyen Anh.

Nguyen Hue is listed by the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism as one of the 14 typical national heroes of Vietnam.[5] Many schools and streets in localities are named Quang Trung and Nguyen Hue.

The king was a man of sagacious intelligence; De Minh loved him dearly and wanted him to succeed to the throne. The king persistently yielded to his older brother and dared not obey the command. De Minh then established De Nghi as the heir to rule the North, and enfeoffed the king as Kinh Duong Vuong to rule the South, calling it the kingdom of Xich Quy.
The king married the daughter of Dong Dinh Quan named Than Long, and fathered Lac Long Quan (Note: The Tang annals record: during the Kinh Duong period, there was a goat-herding woman who claimed to be the youngest daughter of Dong Dinh Quan; she married the second son of Kinh Xuyen but was abandoned, and wrote a letter asking Lieu Nghi to report this to Dong Dinh Quan. Thus, Kinh Xuyen and Dong Dinh had been allied by marriage for generations).

Lac Long Quan
[2a] His taboo name was Sung Lam, son of Kinh Duong Vuong.
The king married De Lai's daughter, Au Co, and fathered a hundred sons (legend has it she gave birth to a hundred eggs), who are the ancestors of the Bach Viet. One day, the king said to Au Co: "I am of the dragon race, you are of the fairy race; water and fire are incompatible, it is truly difficult for us to be together." They then bid each other farewell, dividing 50 children to follow their mother to the mountains, and 50 children to follow their father to the South (some versions record to the South Sea), and enfeoffed the eldest son as Hung Vuong to succeed the throne.
Historian Ngo Si Lien said: When heaven and earth were first formed, there was a being created from vital energy, which was the Pan Gu clan. From the manifestation of energy came the manifestation of physical forms; nothing exists outside the two energies of yin and yang. The I Ching says: "Heaven and earth intermingle, all things are transformed and purified; male and female unite their essences, all things are born." Therefore, there is husband and wife first, then father and son, and after father and son comes ruler and subject. [2b] However, the birth of sages and worthies is always extraordinary, which is due to the mandate of heaven. Swallowing a dark bird's egg to give birth to the Shang dynasty, stepping on a giant's footprint to establish the Zhou dynasty, are all recorded facts of this nature. The descendant of the Than Nong clan, De Minh, married the daughter of Vu Tien and fathered Kinh Duong Vuong, who is the founding ancestor of the Bach Viet. The king married the daughter of Than Long and fathered Lac Long Quan; Lac Long Quan married the daughter of De Lai and had the auspicious blessing of fathering a hundred sons. Is that not what laid the foundation for our Viet nation's enterprise? Examining the Tongjian Waiji (Comprehensive Mirror, Outer Annals), it states: De Lai was the son of De Nghi; according to that record, Kinh Duong Vuong was the biological younger brother of De Nghi, yet they intermarried; perhaps it was because that era was still primitive and rites and music had not yet been established?

Hung Vuong
[3a] The son of Lac Long Quan (taboo name unknown), established the capital in Phong Chau (now Bach Hac district).
Upon ascending the throne, Hung Vuong set the national name as Van Lang (this country bordered the South Sea to the east, Ba Thuc to the west, Dong Dinh lake to the north, and Ho Ton - which is Champa, now Quang Nam - to the south). He divided the country into 15 administrative regions: Giao Chi, Chu Dien, Vu Ninh, Phuc Loc, Viet Thuong, Ninh Hai, Duong Tuyen, Luc Hai, Vu Dinh, Hoai Hoan, Cuu Chan, Binh Van, Tan Hung, Cuu Duc; all were vassal lands of Hung Vuong; while the region called Van Lang was where the king established the capital. He appointed civil generals called Lac Hau, and military generals called Lac Tuong. The king's sons were called Quan Lang, and daughters were called Mi Nuong. Officials in charge of affairs were called Bo Chinh; their hereditary succession from father to son was called phu dao. Kings of all generations were called Hung Vuong. At that time, the people living in the forests and mountains saw that the rivers and streams had shrimp and fish, so they invited each other to catch fish for food, but were often harmed by water monsters (thuong luong). [3b] They came to report this to the king. The king said: "The barbarians in the mountains are different from aquatic species; those aquatic species favor their own kind and hate other species, which is why you are harmed by them." The king then told everyone to use ink to tattoo images of water monsters on their bodies. From then on, the water monsters saw them and no longer bit or harmed them. The tattooing custom of the Bach Viet people probably started from there.

By the time he was over three years old, he ate well and grew big but did not know how to speak or laugh. On that day, the child suddenly spoke, telling his mother to invite the royal envoy in, and said: "Please grant me a sword and a horse, the king needs not worry about anything." The king granted him a sword and a horse; the child immediately rode the horse, brandished the sword, and charged forward with the royal army following behind, defeating the enemy troops at the foot of Vu Ninh mountain. During the reign of King Cheng of Zhou [1063-1026 BC], our country of Viet visited the Zhou dynasty for the first time (it is unclear during which Hung King's reign), claiming to be the Viet Thuong clan, and offered a white pheasant. The Duke of Zhou said: "If our political decrees do not reach them, a gentleman does not treat them as his subjects," and then ordered the construction of a south-pointing chariot to escort the envoys back to their country.

At the end of the Hung Vuong era, the king had a daughter named Mi Nuong, who was remarkably beautiful. Thuc Vuong heard of her and came to propose marriage. The king wanted to agree, but the Hung Hau advised against it: "They want to conquer our country and are only using marriage as an excuse." Because of this, Thuc Vuong harbored resentment. The king, wanting to find a worthy person to marry her to, told his subjects: "This daughter is of fairy descent; only someone with sufficient talent and virtue can be my son-in-law." At that time, two men arrived from outside and bowed in the courtyard to propose. The king found it strange; when asked, they replied that one was [4b] Son Tinh (Mountain Spirit) and the other was Thuy Tinh (Water Spirit), both from the great realm, who had heard the king had a divine daughter and made bold to come request her hand. The king said: "I have only one daughter, how can I have both of you as worthy sons-in-law?" He then set a condition that the next day, whoever brought sufficient betrothal gifts first would marry her. The two men obeyed, bowed in gratitude, and left. The next day, Son Tinh brought jewels, gold, silver, mountain birds, and forest beasts as gifts. The king kept his promise and married his daughter to him. Son Tinh took his wife to live on a high peak of Tan Vien mountain. Thuy Tinh also arrived with betrothal gifts later; furious and regretful that he was too late, he summoned clouds and rain, raised the waters to flood the land, and led aquatic creatures in pursuit. The king and Son Tinh stretched iron nets across the upper reaches of the Tu Liem river to block them. Thuy Tinh took another river, from Ly Nhan to the foot of Quang Oai mountain, then followed the banks up to the Hat river estuary, out to the great river, and turned into the Da river to attack Tan Vien. Everywhere he went, he dug deep abysses and swamps, storing water to plot a surprise attack. Son Tinh possessed divine powers of transformation; he called [5a] the barbarians to weave bamboo into water barriers, and used crossbows to shoot downwards. The scaled and shelled creatures hit by arrows all fled. Ultimately, Thuy Tinh could not invade Tan Vien mountain. (Legend has it that from then on, Son Tinh and Thuy Tinh harbored a generational feud, and every year during the high water season, they often fought each other).

Tan Vien mountain is a high mountain range in our Viet country, and its sacredness is highly responsive. After Mi Nuong married Son Tinh, Thuc Vuong was furious and instructed his descendants to destroy Van Lang and seize the country. In the time of his descendant, Thuc Phan, who possessed courage and strategy, he attacked and conquered the country.

question: How do historians and contemporaries assess Quang Trung's reforms and rule?
answer:
Historians and contemporaries have assessed Quang Trung's reforms and rule as transformative and progressive, emphasizing their impact on Vietnam's political, economic, and cultural development. These assessments are supported by historical records and contemporary accounts.  

### **Historians' Assessments**  
Historian Phan Huy Le highlighted Quang Trung's dual role as a "brilliant military leader" and a "politician with exceptional talent," noting his ability to unify the country and implement reforms that modernized governance. His reforms, which included economic restructuring, educational reforms, and the adoption of Western scientific knowledge, were seen as surpassing contemporary Asian nations. For instance, he reformed taxation and land systems, encouraged handicrafts, and expanded foreign trade with the West. Additionally, he reformed the examination system to prioritize practical knowledge, promoted the use of Vietnamese Nom script over Han script, and eradicated superstitious practices. These measures are described as "progressive tendencies" that ended over a century of stagnation under the Trinh–Nguyen feudal system [Data: Historical Assessments (1, 2); Reforms and Policies (3, 4)].  

### **Contemporary Accounts**  
Contemporaries, including overseas Chinese communities in Hue during the Tay Son era, praised Quang Trung's rule for its fairness and mild governance. A British merchant noted that Quang Trung's administration was "more mildly and fairly" than that of later Nguyen dynasty kings (Gia Long and Minh Mang), reflecting widespread admiration for his leadership [Data: Contemporary Accounts (5); Overseas Chinese Testimonies (6)].  

### **Legacy and Impact**  
Quang Trung's reforms are credited with laying the foundation for national reunification under the Tay Son Dynasty. His military strategies, including victories against Siamese and Qing invaders, solidified his reputation as a formidable leader. However, his sudden death at 39 and the subsequent decline of the Tay Son Dynasty underscored the challenges of sustaining such reforms. Despite this, his legacy endures, with institutions like schools and streets named after him, and his rule remains a symbol of progressive governance in Vietnamese history [Data: Reforms and Policies (7); Legacy and Recognition (8, 9)].  

These assessments collectively underscore Quang Trung's significance as a unifying figure whose reforms bridged traditional and modern governance, leaving a lasting imprint on Vietnam's historical trajectory.
